label: Button
title: Button
summary: Use Button when one clear action moves someone forward, confirms a choice, or completes a task.
corePrinciple: Make the action clear before choosing its appearance. The label should explain what happens next.

anatomy.title: Four purposeful parts
anatomy.description: Keep the component simple. The label is required; the start slot and end icon are supporting tools. Most actions need one at most, and many need neither.
blocks: Holds the action and resolves its visual treatment.
Optional. Use for an icon that clarifies the action.
Required. Name the outcome in one to three words.
Optional. Use when direction or continuation matters.

configuration.title: Choose type by context
configuration.description: Type sets the component’s structure. Appearance and emphasis then express hierarchy and meaning.
blocks: The standard solid action. It hugs its label or fills its container when the layout asks it to.
Keeps long content within the system width limit. It remains responsive rather than using a hand-set pixel width.
A translucent action for rich media or coloured surfaces. Its backdrop is part of the result.
Use only over a meaningful backdrop
Appearance identifies the family. Emphasis decides how loudly the action speaks within that family.
Reserve these appearances for an outcome with clear positive, warning, or negative meaning.

states.title: States respond to what is happening
states.description: Idle, hover, and pressed communicate interaction. Disabled and loading communicate availability while content is prepared.
blocks: Appears while the action is held.
Unavailable until a condition is met.
A shape-preserving skeleton holds the action’s place.
Design the cause, not just the state.
Hover and pressed happen automatically. Disabled should have a clear condition. Use loading while required content is being prepared, not as a substitute for transaction progress.

sizing.title: Match size to prominence and density
sizing.description: Size is a deliberate component choice. Width is resolved by the layout and available container space.
blocks: The action leads a screen, sheet, or key step.
The action sits inside a card or compact group.
Space is dense and the surrounding touch area stays usable.
Keep the action close to the content it completes.
The same action can fill the available width.
Container width resolves the layout. Designers choose the label, hierarchy, and size—not a separate “desktop” or “mobile” Button.

content.title: Name the outcome
content.description: A person should understand what will happen before pressing the button.
blocks: Use clear actions such as “Save details”, “Transfer money”, or “View statement”.
Aim for one to three words. Put explanation beside the button, not inside it.
Add one only when it improves recognition, direction, or the action’s meaning.
Prefer “Pay ₹500” or “Download report” over a vague “OK” when the outcome can be named.

inContext.title: Place the action where the decision happens
inContext.description: Use surrounding content to explain the choice. Let the button stay concise.
blocks: Flexible access with no lock-in period.
The stronger action carries the decision.
Track every goal in one view

doDont.title: Protect clarity and hierarchy
doDont.description: These pairs show the common choices that make Button easier—or harder—to understand.
blocks: The outcome is clear before the action is pressed.
Put the explanation inside the button
Long labels are slower to scan and can truncate.
The hierarchy tells people where to go next.
Two dominant actions make the choice harder to read.
Use Default when a footer action fills the container
The layout owns the width while Button keeps its system shape.
Use Fixed as a substitute for a full-width action
Fixed is bounded by the system and will not behave like Fill.
Use Glass over a visible backdrop
Translucency has a clear relationship with the surface.
Place Glass on a plain, low-contrast surface
The treatment loses its purpose and can become hard to read.

sources.title: Grounded in the published component
sources.description: This guide separates designer choices from behaviour supplied by the product at runtime.
blocks: Live examples use the public Coin Button from jfs-components 0.1.60. Hover and pressed feedback are supplied by the component; loading uses its shape-preserving skeleton.
